extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and students of literature and theatre interested in comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for creating and judging comic writing (comedy, comic poetry, satire, irony, and humour), with examples and distinctions among related modes. Emphasises how the Comic spirit operates in society, on stage, and in literary characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comic (the governing spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic, which is the perceptive, is the governing spirit, awakening and giving aim to powers of laughter; it enfolds thinner forms of satire, irony, and humour but differs from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Comic addresses the intellect rather than the feelings. It quickens the intellect to detect comedy by presenting contrasts between characters and the wiser world about them. It does not sharply drive into quivering sensibilities (satire) nor does it comfort and tuck up sensibilities (humour); rather it offers a subtler, intellectual perception of social life. Examples: Alceste and Tartuffe are described as 'purely comic, addressed to the intellect.' Fielding’s look upon Richardson is essentially comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire is the mode of detecting ridicule and attacking the ridiculous person — 'slipping into the grasp of Satire' when kindliness is chilled by ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire is a moral agent, 'often a social scavenger, working on a storage of bile.' It drives blows into the sensibilities — the laughter of satire is 'a blow in the back or the face.' It commonly has a moral object and can be savage (e.g., Swift). Avoid conflating satire with the Comic: satire aims to wound or reform rather than merely to illuminate a comic perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony is the device of stinging under a semi-caress so that the subject is left dubious whether anything has hurt — 'an engine of Irony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony can be savage with moral purpose (Swift) or sedate and malicious (Gibbon). It is 'the humour of satire' and may vary by caprice. Beware 'foppish irony' that frets to be seen and 'irony which leers' that fails by being too explicit; such affects are failures when they pretend to ambiguity but reveal intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is a spirit that laughs round a figure, spares and pities while exposing; it refreshes feelings and sometimes allows feelings to be too much for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humourist of mean order is a refreshing laugher with feelings primary; the humourist of high order embraces contrasts beyond the Comic and may fuse Tragic sentiment with Comic narrative (e.g., Don Quixote, Yorick). Humour comforts and shows compassion, differing from satire's cruelty and the Comic's intellectual address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction among Comic, Satire, Irony, and Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic, Satire, Irony, and Humour are related but distinct modes: the Comic is perceptive and intellectual; satire wounds and moralises; irony injects ambiguity and indirect sting; humour consolingly spares and enfolds feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct classification depends on the authorial intention and effect on the audience: e.g., Jonathan Wild’s protest is 'immensely comic' rather than satiric; the same character, presented with a different stance, becomes satiric. Misreading (calling Comedy ironic or satiric) often reflects the reader's choice to see irony in life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic poet's scope and focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic poet works in the narrow field of the society he depicts and addresses 'the still narrower enclosure of men's intellects' with reference to social operations on character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic poets are not concerned with extensive beginnings, endings, or surroundings; they focus on the present 'weaving' of social life. To value the work, readers must have 'a sober liking of your kind' and a sober estimate of civilized qualities. Examples include Molière's comedies and Shakespeare's comic scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of true Comedy — awaken thoughtful laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of true Comedy is that it shall awaken thoughtful laughter: comedy should 'awaken thoughtful laughter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy should quicken the mind; its laughter is 'the humour of the mind' and often more like a polite smile than a noisy roar. A flourishing Comic idea in a society is taken as a sign of civilisation. Comedy's purpose is intellectual illumination via laughter rather than mere amusement or derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of comic laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy’s laughter is impersonal, polite, and near a smile; it 'laughs through the mind' and is not a savage or derisive shout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subtle, mentally-directed laughter to loud derision. The comic laugh 'entrances' and 'finely tempers' emotion, showing 'mental richness rather than noisy enormity.' This is an aesthetic criterion when judging comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding derision — what makes ridicule uncomic
rubrics_metrics.description: Derisive laughter that casts ridicule on unfortunate nature rather than exposed convention thwarts the Comic idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents that provoke derision (ridiculing misfortune or poverty without perceiving the comic contrast) are 'too gross for Comedy.' The Comic perception prefers laughing at pretension or conceit — e.g., Caleb Balderstone's attempt to make rags conceal bareness is comic — whereas simple misery is not comic unless it produces pretentious attempts at decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mesure et goût — restraint and taste in Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy must be 'kept in restraint'; the French stress 'mesure et goût' (measure and taste) as essential to good comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy benefits from discipline and moderation; Molière is credited with leading French taste toward simple justness and restraint. Avoid gross or excessive treatment that would make comic scenes farcical rather than intellectually illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humourist of high order: fusion with Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The great humourist fuses Tragedy with the Comic: 'The stroke of the great humourist is world-wide, with lights of Tragedy in his laughter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High humour can evoke both compassion and derision and thus produces a richer response (heart and mind laugh together, as in Don Quixote). This is a criterion for evaluating the depth of humour: does it embrace contrasts that elevate the comic to universal human insight?

rubrics_metrics.name: Humourist of mean order — primary feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The humourist of mean order is a refreshing laugher who gives tone to feelings and sometimes allows feelings to overwhelm him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such humourists are pleasing but limited; their work relies on feeling rather than intellectual distance. Recognise the difference when assessing humour: immediate emotional effect versus sustained intellectual comic perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: The role of character juxtaposition (contrast) in Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often depends on the contrast between characters (e.g., knight and squire in Don Quixote) which quickens the intellect to detect comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how effectively the author uses oppositions to reveal comic truth: the more sharply the contrast exposes folly or pretension while retaining humane sympathy, the more successful the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic spirit as social and civilising test
rubrics_metrics.description: A flourishing Comic idea and Comedy in a country is a test of the civilisation of that country; sensitivity to the comic laugh is a step in civilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence and quality of comic literature and social temper as an indicator of social refinement. The essay suggests that nations schooled in writers like Molière, La Bruyère, and La Fontaine develop beneficial comic traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy vs realism — benefits of enclosing the Comic idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclosing the Comic idea in a comedy (as opposed to raw realism) makes it more perceptible and portable; realism's crude directness can produce collisions in scenes and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern French realism's direct study of life can create crude collisions and produce 'Aventurière' archetypes; by contrast, comedy framed by the Comic idea presents lessons in a more portable and broadly understood way. For writers: enclosing comic perception in a clear scheme aids audience reception and moral balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-writing discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing for the stage enforces a definite plan and economy of expression: 'Writing for the stage would be a corrective of a too-incrusted scholarly style... keeps minor writers to a definite plan, and to English.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwriting requires clarity of scheme and immediacy, training writers in restraint and intelligible expression. This is a practical production criterion: stage work disciplines prose and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks when humour, satire and irony hunt together
rubrics_metrics.description: Humourist and Satirist frequently hunt together as Ironeïsts in pursuit of the grotesque, to the exclusion of the Comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When humour, satire, and irony combine to chase grotesque subjects, they may exclude the Comic spirit's intellectual restraint and produce less salutary effects. Evaluate works for balance: do they preserve the Comic's intellectuality or descend into mere grotesque, sensational, or bitter attack?

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader predisposition affects interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers who 'detect irony in Comedy do so because they choose to see it in life' — interpretation often reflects the reader's habits of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a work is comic, satiric, ironic, or humorous, account for reader bias; misattribution of tone may not be the author's fault but the audience's inclination to interpret life ironically or sentimentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic spirit's ethical moderation and fellowship
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic spirit tempers wrath and spares the need for harsh blows; it confers fellowship, lowers personal pride, and 'is not hostile to the sweetest songfully poetic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy's moral effect is to moderate pride and to offer 'a harmless wine' that conduces to sobriety. Evaluate comic works for their humane moderation: do they enlighten without cruelty and produce social fellowship rather than vindictiveness?
